analysis.one_liner: Temporarily boosts Social Security checks, sets a higher minimum for low earners, and loosens SSI limits.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2020 with 83 Democratic cosponsors including the Ways and Means chairman, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised Social Security payments for 2020, corrected a formula quirk that would have quietly cut future benefit calculations because average wages fell during the COVID recession, and created a higher minimum benefit for people who worked long careers at low wages. It also extended children's benefits to full-time college students, improved widows' and widowers' benefits, eased rules for children raised by grandparents and other relatives, and temporarily raised the income and savings limits for Supplemental Security Income. The increased benefits would have been paid out of the general Treasury fund rather than through any new tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security and disability beneficiaries, who would have received a one-year increase in their monthly checks and protection from the COVID-era wage-index formula cut; lifetime low earners with at least 11 years of work, who would have gotten a minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line; widows and widowers in two-income households; full-time college students up to age 22 who lose a parent; children living with grandparents or other relatives under court custody; and SSI recipients, whose income and savings limits would have been temporarily raised.

how_it_helps.text: Uses the highest prior-year national average wage index when it is higher than the COVID-depressed 2020 figure, preventing a formula-driven drop in benefit calculations [S3 Sec. 3; S2].

Raises the across-the-board benefit factor from 90 to 93 percent for calendar year 2020, an increase for all beneficiaries, and requires the Social Security Commissioner to recompute benefits and pay any underpayments quickly [S3 Sec. 4, 13].
Creates a minimum benefit for long-term low earners, rising with each year of work from 6.25 percent of the poverty guideline at 11 years up to 125 percent at 30 or more years [S3 Sec. 5].

Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $35,000 for single filers and $50,000 for joint filers, keeping more of recipients' benefits out of federal income tax [S3 Sec. 6].
Extends children's benefits to full-time post-secondary students through age 23, up from benefits generally ending after high school [S3 Sec. 7; S2].
Improves widow's and widower's benefits in two-income households by allowing up to 75 percent of the combined old-age and survivor benefit [S3 Sec. 8; S2].

Lets children living with grandparents or other relatives qualify for benefits based on living with and being supported by that relative, including where a court has granted custody, instead of requiring adoption [S3 Sec. 9; S2].

Temporarily raises SSI general and earned income exclusions and doubles the individual and couple resource limits for 2020, excludes in-kind support from income, and holds SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries harmless so higher Social Security payments do not cost them other benefits [S3 Sec. 10, 11, 12].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and the Treasury: the bill appropriates whatever sums are needed from the general fund into the Social Security trust funds to pay for the increases, with no new tax or revenue offset. It also forgoes federal income tax revenue by raising the thresholds at which benefits are taxed. The Medicare hospital insurance trust fund is specifically held harmless from the tax-threshold change.

drawbacks.text: The bill is deficit-financed: it appropriates from the general fund of the Treasury to cover all the benefit increases with no new revenue source [S3 Sec. 14].
The across-the-board increase goes to every beneficiary regardless of financial need, including higher-income retirees [S3 Sec. 4].

Most provisions are written to apply to calendar year 2020 only, including the SSI limit increases, the child-student extension, and the widow(er) benefit improvement, making the relief temporary rather than structural [S3 Sec. 7(e), 8(c), 10].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and well-targeted in places: the low-earner minimum, widow(er) fix, kinship-care expansion, and SSI loosening concentrate help on people with the least, and the bill explicitly protects SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP eligibility from being reduced because of the higher payments. The honest cost is that the whole package is deficit-financed with no offset, and the flat 3% boost reaches affluent retirees as well as struggling ones. The temporary 2020-only design also means the emergency relief would have evaporated the following year rather than fixing the low-benefit problem permanently.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees in July 2020, never received a committee vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 9, 2020 by Rep. John Larson with 82 original cosponsors plus himself, all Democrats [S3].
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and within Ways and Means to the Subcommittees on Select Revenue Measures and Social Security [S1; S5].
No further action was ever taken: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the near term, the federal Treasury, since no general-fund appropriation for the benefit increases ever occurred. Social Security and SSI beneficiaries got nothing: no benefit increase, no low-earner minimum, and no protection from the COVID-era wage-index formula cut.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.role: Sponsor; Chair, Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 9, 2020 to prevent a COVID-driven benefit cut and raise benefits on an emergency basis

for.name: Rep. Richard E. Neal
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor at introduction

for.name: 83 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote; the bill stayed at the subcommittee-referral stage for the rest of the Congress

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Held majority control and floor scheduling power in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: All 83 cosponsors were House Democrats, including the Ways and Means chairman; no Republican signed on, and the bill received no committee or floor vote where positions could be recorded.
